lessons.title: Voltage, current, resistance and power
lessons.summary: The four quantities behind every circuit, Ohm's law and P = VI, unit prefixes, ground as a reference, complete circuits, and which way current "flows".
lessons.body:
Every circuit in a synth, from an LED on the front panel to the board's audio output, obeys a few simple rules. Learn them well now and the rest of this module is mostly applying them.

> [!warning] Low voltage only
> This module covers low-voltage DC work only: USB power, bench supplies of a few volts, and batteries. It does **not** cover mains wiring or mains power supplies. Use a ready-made, certified supply (a USB charger or a bench supply) and never open or modify anything that plugs into the wall.

## Four quantities

**Voltage** (V, measured in volts) is the difference in electrical potential between two points. It is the "push". A voltage is always *between* two points. "This pin is at 3.3 V" really means "3.3 V higher than ground".

**Current** (I, measured in amperes or amps, A) is the rate at which charge flows past a point. One amp is one coulomb per second. Current flows *through* things.

**Resistance** (R, measured in ohms, Ω) is how strongly something opposes current. A resistor is a part made to have a known resistance.

**Power** (P, measured in watts, W) is the rate at which energy is transferred, for example turned into heat in a resistor or into light in an LED.

A water analogy helps at first: voltage is pressure, current is flow rate, and resistance is a narrow pipe. Don't push it too far. It breaks down for capacitors and for anything at audio or radio frequencies.

## Ohm's law

For a resistor, the voltage across it is proportional to the current through it:

```
V = I × R
I = V / R
R = V / I
```

If you know any two, you can find the third. A 1 kΩ resistor with 5 V across it carries 5 / 1000 = 5 mA.

Ohm's law describes resistors (and wires). It does not describe LEDs and diodes. Their current rises steeply once the voltage passes a threshold, so you can't use "V / R" on an LED directly. You use it on the resistor in series with the LED, as in the worked example below.

## Power: P = VI

Power is voltage times current. Substituting Ohm's law gives two more forms that are useful for resistors:

```
P = V × I
P = I² × R
P = V² / R
```

Power matters because resistors, regulators and chips all have a maximum they can dissipate before they overheat. A typical small through-hole resistor is rated at 0.25 W (check the actual part's datasheet).

> [!example] An LED's resistor
> A 5 V supply drives an LED through a 330 Ω resistor, and you measure 10 mA. The resistor drops 10 mA × 330 Ω = 3.3 V and dissipates 3.3 V × 10 mA = 33 mW. That is well inside a 0.25 W (250 mW) rating. The remaining 1.7 V is across the LED.

```python
# LED budget on a 5 V supply
V_supply = 5.0
I = 0.010          # 10 mA
R = 330.0          # ohms

V_R = I * R        # Ohm's law
P_R = V_R * I      # P = VI
print(f"V across R: {V_R:.2f} V")
print(f"Power in R: {P_R*1000:.1f} mW")
V_led = V_supply - V_R  # KVL
print(f"Left for LED: {V_led:.2f} V")
```

```
V across R: 3.30 V
Power in R: 33.0 mW
Left for LED: 1.70 V
```

## Units and prefixes

Electronics spans huge ranges, so SI prefixes are everywhere. Get them wrong and you're off by a factor of a thousand.

| Prefix | Symbol | Factor |
|---|---|---|
| mega | M | 10⁶ |
| kilo | k | 10³ |
| milli | m | 10⁻³ |
| micro | µ (or u) | 10⁻⁶ |
| nano | n | 10⁻⁹ |
| pico | p | 10⁻¹² |

Tips:

- Note the case: **m** (milli) and **M** (mega) differ by 10⁹.
- Schematics often put the prefix where the decimal point would be: `4k7` = 4.7 kΩ, `2R2` = 2.2 Ω, `100n` = 100 nF.
- A handy pairing: volts ÷ kilohms = milliamps. 3.3 V across 1 kΩ is 3.3 mA.

## Complete circuits

Current only flows around a **closed loop**: from the supply's positive terminal, through the load, and back to the supply's negative terminal. Break the loop anywhere (an open switch, a loose jumper, a cracked solder joint) and the current everywhere in that loop drops to zero.

```diagram
 +5V ---[ R 330 ]---[ LED >| ]---+
  |                              |
 supply                          |
  |                              |
 0V -----------------------------+
          return path (ground)
```

Two consequences:

- **The return path is part of the circuit.** A signal that leaves your synth board on one wire must come back on another. With audio cables, the sleeve or shield is that return.
- **Current is the same everywhere in a single loop.** If 10 mA flows through the resistor, 10 mA flows through the LED. This is Kirchhoff's current law in its simplest form.

Kirchhoff's voltage law is the other half: around any closed loop, the voltage rises equal the drops. In the LED circuit, 5 V = 3.3 V (resistor) + 1.7 V (LED).

## Ground is a reference

**Ground** (GND, 0 V) is the point you choose to measure every other voltage against. In a battery- or USB-powered synth it's usually the supply's negative terminal. It doesn't have to connect to the earth in the soil.

Three meanings of "ground" get mixed up:

- **Signal or circuit ground:** the 0 V reference and return path inside your circuit. This is what "GND" on a microcontroller board means.
- **Chassis ground:** the conductive case or chassis reference; whether it connects to circuit 0 V depends on the equipment design.
- **Protective earth:** the mains safety earth in a wall socket. It belongs to mains equipment and is not something to modify. Lesson 7 returns to this.

Two practical rules follow:

1. **Direct, non-isolated single-ended signals need a shared reference.** For ordinary GPIO/UART links, connect the boards' GND pins. Isolated links such as DIN MIDI deliberately avoid a direct ground connection. A voltage only means something relative to a reference both sides agree on.
2. **"0 V" isn't the same everywhere.** Ground wires have small resistances. When current flows through them, two "ground" points can differ by a few millivolts. For audio that's enough to hear (lesson 7).

## Conventional current and electron flow

Circuit diagrams and textbooks use **conventional current**: current flows from + to −. That convention predates the discovery of the electron. In a metal wire the charge carriers are actually electrons, which are negative and drift the opposite way, from − to +.

Both descriptions predict the same voltages, currents and power. Every formula, datasheet and schematic symbol uses conventional current. A forward-biased diode carries conventional current from anode to cathode (the bar). An LED's outward arrows indicate light, not current. Use conventional current and treat electron flow as a physics detail.

## Pitfalls

- **Measuring a voltage "at a point" without a reference.** Always know which two points you mean. Usually one of them is ground.
- **Forgetting the return path.** A direct single-ended GPIO signal needs its reference/return; isolated interfaces use a different return arrangement.
- **Ignoring power.** A resistor that's correct by Ohm's law can still cook if P = I²R exceeds its rating.
- **Prefix slips.** 1 MΩ instead of 1 kΩ is a thousand-fold error. Write values with their units every time.

## Key takeaways

- Voltage is between two points, current flows through a component, resistance opposes current, and power is energy per second.
- Ohm's law V = IR applies to resistors. Use it on the resistor, not on an LED or diode.
- P = VI = I²R = V²/R. Check every resistor against its power rating.
- Current needs a complete loop, and the return path is part of the circuit.
- Ground is the reference you measure against. Connected devices must share it.
- Use conventional current (+ to −). Electron flow is the physical reality in wires but gives the same answers.
- This module stays at low voltage. Never work on mains.

questions.prompt: A 9 V battery is connected across a single 4.7 kΩ resistor. Roughly what current flows?

options.text: About 19 mA
options.explanation: This treats 4.7 kΩ as 470 Ω, a factor-of-ten prefix slip. 9 / 470 ≈ 19 mA, but the resistor is 4700 Ω.

options.text: About 42 A
options.explanation: This multiplies instead of dividing (9 × 4.7). Ohm's law gives I = V / R, not V × R.

options.text: About 0.52 mA
options.explanation: This is R / V (4.7 / 9). The ratio is inverted; current falls as resistance rises.

options.text: About 1.9 mA
options.explanation: Correct. I = V / R = 9 V / 4700 Ω ≈ 0.0019 A = 1.9 mA.

questions.workedExample:
1. Write Ohm's law for current: `I = V / R`.
2. Convert the prefix: 4.7 kΩ = 4700 Ω.
3. Divide: 9 / 4700 = 0.001915 A.
4. Convert to milliamps: × 1000 = 1.915 mA, about 1.9 mA.

Shortcut: volts ÷ kilohms gives milliamps directly, so 9 ÷ 4.7 ≈ 1.9 mA.

questions.prompt: A schematic labels a capacitor `100n`. What value is that?

options.text: 0.1 µF
options.explanation: Correct. 100 nF = 100 × 10⁻⁹ F = 10⁻⁷ F = 0.1 µF. Both forms appear on schematics and parts lists.

options.text: 100 µF
options.explanation: µ is 10⁻⁶ and n is 10⁻⁹. 100 µF would be a thousand times larger than 100 nF.

options.text: 100 mF
options.explanation: m (milli, 10⁻³) is a different prefix; 100 mF would be a huge capacitor and is a million times larger.

options.text: 100 pF
options.explanation: p is 10⁻¹², a thousand times smaller than n.

questions.workedExample:
1. `n` means nano, 10⁻⁹.
2. 100 nF = 100 × 10⁻⁹ F = 1 × 10⁻⁷ F.
3. In microfarads (10⁻⁶ F): 10⁻⁷ / 10⁻⁶ = 0.1 µF.

So 100n, 100 nF and 0.1 µF are the same part. This is the value commonly used for decoupling, which you will meet in lesson 4.

questions.prompt: You measure 2.5 mA through a resistor with 5 V across it. What is its resistance?

options.explanation: This multiplies 5 × 2.5, mixing a product with the units. Ohm's law gives R = V / I.
This forgets that 2.5 mA is 0.0025 A, a milli-prefix slip.

options.text: 2 kΩ

options.explanation: This is out by a factor of 10. 5 / 0.0025 = 2000.

questions.workedExample:
1. R = V / I.
2. Convert: 2.5 mA = 0.0025 A.
3. R = 5 / 0.0025 = 2000 Ω = 2 kΩ.

Shortcut: volts ÷ milliamps gives kilohms: 5 ÷ 2.5 = 2 kΩ.

questions.prompt: For a battery driving a forward-biased LED through a resistor, which statement about conventional current and the LED symbol is correct?

options.text: From − to +, because the arrow follows the electrons
options.explanation: Electrons in a wire do drift from − to +, but schematics and formulas use conventional current, which goes the other way.

options.text: Conventional current flows through the load from + to − and through the LED from anode to cathode; its outward arrows show light
options.explanation: Correct. The cathode is marked by the bar; LED emission arrows describe light.

options.text: It doesn't matter, because AC and DC circuits use opposite conventions
options.explanation: The convention is the same for AC and DC. In AC the direction alternates, but the reference direction is still defined using conventional current.

options.text: The LED's outward arrows show electron flow
options.explanation: Those arrows show light emission. Electrons in metal move opposite conventional current.

questions.workedExample:
1. Conventional current is defined in the direction of positive-charge flow: through the external load from battery + to −.
2. In the forward-biased LED it flows from anode to cathode (the bar).
3. The LED symbol's small outward arrows represent emitted light. They are not current arrows.

questions.prompt: You put a 100 Ω, 0.25 W resistor directly across a 5 V supply. What happens, and what should you do?

options.text: Nothing to worry about: 50 mA is a small current
options.explanation: Small for a supply, maybe, but the resistor's power is what matters. 5 V × 50 mA = 0.25 W, right at the rating.

options.text: It dissipates 0.25 W, at its maximum rating, so it runs hot. Use a higher-wattage part or a larger resistance
options.explanation: Correct. P = V²/R = 25/100 = 0.25 W. Running a part continuously at its absolute limit is poor practice; leave margin (often half the rating or less) by using a 0.5 W part or a larger resistor.

options.text: It dissipates 2.5 W and burns out immediately
options.explanation: This multiplies V by R and divides by 10, or similar. P = V²/R = 25 / 100 = 0.25 W, not 2.5 W.

options.text: It dissipates 0.05 W because P = V / R
options.explanation: V / R is the current (0.05 A), not the power. Power is V × I.

questions.workedExample:
1. Current: I = V / R = 5 / 100 = 0.05 A = 50 mA.
2. Power: P = V × I = 5 × 0.05 = 0.25 W. Check with P = V²/R = 25 / 100 = 0.25 W.
3. Compare with the rating: 0.25 W of 0.25 W, so 100%.
4. A resistor at its full rating gets hot and its life and accuracy suffer. Choose a 0.5 W part, or ask whether you really need that much current.

questions.prompt: An LED circuit is: 3.3 V → 220 Ω resistor → red LED → ground. The LED datasheet gives a forward voltage of about 2.0 V at the current of interest. Approximately what current flows?

options.text: 15 mA
options.explanation: This is 3.3 V / 220 Ω, which ignores the voltage dropped by the LED. Only the resistor's share of the voltage sets the current through the resistor.

options.text: 9.1 mA
options.explanation: This is 2.0 V / 220 Ω. The resistor sees the supply minus the LED voltage, not the LED voltage.

options.text: It can't be estimated because LEDs don't obey Ohm's law
options.explanation: Ohm's law doesn't apply to the LED, but it does apply to the resistor. Using the LED's forward voltage gives a good estimate.

options.text: About 5.9 mA
options.explanation: Correct. The resistor has 3.3 − 2.0 = 1.3 V across it, so I = 1.3 / 220 ≈ 5.9 mA. The same current flows through the LED because it's a single loop.

questions.workedExample:
1. Kirchhoff's voltage law around the loop: 3.3 V = V_R + V_LED.
2. V_R = 3.3 − 2.0 = 1.3 V.
3. Ohm's law on the resistor: I = 1.3 / 220 = 0.0059 A ≈ 5.9 mA.
4. Single loop, so the LED carries the same 5.9 mA.

The real forward voltage shifts a little with current and temperature, so this is an estimate. Measure it to confirm.

questions.prompt: Your LED circuit works on the breadboard. You unplug the jumper that connects the LED's cathode back to ground. What is the current through the resistor now?

options.text: Zero, because the loop is broken
options.explanation: Correct. Current only flows around a complete loop. Breaking it anywhere, even on the ground side, stops current everywhere in that loop.

options.text: Unchanged, because the resistor is still connected to +3.3 V
options.explanation: Being connected to the supply at one end isn't enough. Without a return path no charge can flow.

options.text: Higher, because the LED is no longer dropping voltage
options.explanation: With no current, nothing drops any voltage. There's no path, so there's no current at all.

options.text: Half, because only one side of the circuit is connected
options.explanation: Current isn't shared out by how many ends are connected. A loop is either complete or it isn't.

questions.workedExample:
1. Trace the loop: + → resistor → LED → jumper → ground → back to the supply.
2. Remove the jumper and the loop is open.
3. With an open loop, I = 0 everywhere in it.
4. A consequence: with no current, there's no voltage drop across the resistor, so both its ends and the LED's anode now sit at 3.3 V. A meter shows 3.3 V at the LED's anode, which can confuse you when debugging.

questions.prompt: Which statements about ground are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Ground is the reference point other voltages are measured against
options.explanation: Correct. "This pin is at 3.3 V" means 3.3 V relative to ground.

options.text: Two boards connected by ordinary non-isolated single-ended GPIO signals need a shared ground reference
options.explanation: Correct for this connection. Isolated interfaces such as DIN MIDI deliberately do not join their circuit grounds.

options.text: Ground in a USB-powered circuit must be wired to the earth pin of a wall socket
options.explanation: Circuit ground is just the 0 V reference, usually the supply's negative terminal. Protective earth belongs to mains equipment, which you should leave alone.

options.text: Every ground point in a circuit is at exactly 0 V at all times
options.explanation: Ground conductors have resistance. Current through them produces small voltage differences between "ground" points, which matters for audio.

questions.workedExample:
Check each statement against the lesson:

1. Reference: yes, by definition.
2. Shared ground: yes for ordinary direct single-ended GPIO; isolated links are an exception. A signal is a voltage relative to a reference. If two boards don't share one, the receiver measures against the wrong reference.
3. Earth pin: no. Circuit ground and protective earth are different things.
4. Exactly 0 V: no. A 0.05 Ω ground wire carrying 100 mA has 5 mV across it.

questions.prompt: A ground wire between two boards has 0.05 Ω of resistance and carries 200 mA of supply return current. Board B reads a signal from board A, measuring it against its own ground. By how much can B's reading be off?

options.text: 0 V, because ground is 0 V by definition
options.explanation: Each board's ground is a reference, but the wire between them has resistance. Current through it creates a voltage difference.

options.text: 4 V
options.explanation: This divides 0.2 by 0.05. Ohm's law is V = I × R, not I / R.

options.text: 10 mV
options.explanation: Correct. V = I × R = 0.2 × 0.05 = 0.01 V = 10 mV. That's the offset between the two grounds and therefore the error in B's measurement.

options.text: 2 mV
options.explanation: This uses 0.2 × 0.01 or a similar slip. 200 mA × 50 mΩ = 10 mV.

questions.workedExample:
1. The return current flows through the ground wire's resistance.
2. Voltage across the wire: V = I × R = 0.2 A × 0.05 Ω = 0.01 V = 10 mV.
3. Board A's ground is therefore 10 mV away from board B's.
4. B measures A's signal plus or minus that 10 mV.

For a logic signal with volts of margin this doesn't matter. For audio it does. A changing return current, such as a processor's or LED's, puts its pattern into the audio as noise. Lesson 7 covers fixes.

questions.prompt: Which statements about power in resistors are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Doubling the voltage across a fixed resistor quadruples its power
options.explanation: Correct. P = V²/R, so 2× the voltage gives 4× the power. This is why small voltage increases can overheat a part.

options.text: For a fixed current, a larger resistor dissipates more power
options.explanation: Correct. P = I²R; at fixed current, power is proportional to R.

options.text: For a fixed voltage, a larger resistor dissipates more power
options.explanation: At fixed voltage P = V²/R, so a larger R dissipates *less*. Whether power rises or falls with R depends on what is held constant.

options.text: P = VI applies only to resistors
options.explanation: P = VI applies to any component: resistors, LEDs, chips. The I²R and V²/R forms are the ones that need Ohm's law and so apply to resistors.

questions.workedExample:
1. From P = V²/R: (2V)²/R = 4V²/R, so power quadruples.
2. From P = I²R: at fixed I, P scales with R.
3. From P = V²/R: at fixed V, P scales with 1/R, so a larger R means less power.
4. P = VI is the general definition of electrical power for any two-terminal part. Substituting Ohm's law gives the resistor-only forms.

questions.prompt: A beginner connects an LED straight from a 3.3 V microcontroller pin to ground, with no resistor, reasoning that "3.3 V is low, so it's safe". Why is this a bad idea?

options.text: Above its forward voltage an LED's current rises very steeply, so nothing but the pin's internal resistance limits it. The current can exceed the pin's or LED's rating
options.explanation: Correct. An LED isn't a resistor. Once the voltage exceeds its forward voltage, a small extra voltage drives a big extra current. A series resistor sets the current.

options.text: LEDs need at least 5 V, so it simply won't light
options.explanation: Many LEDs, red ones especially, light well below 3.3 V. The risk isn't failure to light but too much current.

options.text: It's fine as long as the LED is red
options.explanation: Colour changes the forward voltage, but every LED has the same steep curve. Without a resistor the current is still uncontrolled.

options.text: The LED will reverse-bias and block all current
options.explanation: Connected anode to pin and cathode to ground, the LED is forward biased. Reverse bias is the wrong way round and is a different problem.

questions.workedExample:
1. Resistors obey V = IR: current is proportional to voltage.
2. LEDs and diodes don't. Near the forward voltage, current rises roughly exponentially with voltage.
3. With 3.3 V applied to a red LED rated at about 2 V, nothing sets the current except the pin driver's internal resistance and the LED's own resistance.
4. The resulting current can exceed the pin's maximum (see the board's datasheet) and the LED's rating.
5. Fix: a series resistor sized with R = (V_supply − V_f) / I, as in lesson 3.

lessons.title: Series, parallel and voltage dividers
lessons.summary: Combining resistors, the voltage divider formula, why loading a divider changes its output, and how a knob on a synth is just a divider with a moving tap.
lessons.body:
Every knob on a microcontroller synth is a voltage divider. The board reads the voltage at the knob's middle pin with an ADC and turns it into a number. To wire knobs correctly, and to understand why some readings come out wrong, you need series and parallel resistance and the divider formula.

## Series: one path, resistances add

Components in **series** share a single current path. The same current flows through each one, and their voltages add up to the total.

```
R_total = R1 + R2 + R3 + ...
```

A 1 kΩ and a 2.2 kΩ in series behave like one 3.2 kΩ resistor. The series total is always larger than the largest part.

## Parallel: several paths, conductances add

Components in **parallel** connect across the same two nodes, so they all have the **same voltage**. The currents split between the branches and add up to the total.

```
1/R_total = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + ...

two resistors:
R_total = (R1 × R2) / (R1 + R2)
```

Three facts are worth memorising:

- Two equal resistors in parallel give half the value: 10 kΩ ∥ 10 kΩ = 5 kΩ.
- The parallel total is always **smaller than the smallest** branch.
- A much larger resistor in parallel barely changes anything: 10 kΩ ∥ 1 MΩ ≈ 9.9 kΩ.

The symbol ∥ means "in parallel with".

## The voltage divider

Two resistors in series across a supply split the voltage in proportion to their resistances. The output is taken from the junction:

```diagram
 Vin ──┐
       R1
       ├──── Vout
       R2
 GND ──┘
```

Because the same current I = Vin / (R1 + R2) flows through both resistors, the voltage across R2 is I × R2:

```
Vout = Vin × R2 / (R1 + R2)
```

Examples:

- R1 = R2: Vout = Vin / 2. Two 10 kΩ across 3.3 V give 1.65 V.
- R1 = 20 kΩ, R2 = 10 kΩ from 5 V: Vout = 5 × 10/30 ≈ 1.67 V.
- The ratio sets the output, not the absolute values. 1 kΩ/1 kΩ and 100 kΩ/100 kΩ both halve the voltage when unloaded.

The absolute values still matter in two ways. They set the standing current (and so the wasted power), and they determine how badly the output sags when something draws current from it.

## Loading: the divider's output changes when you use it

The formula assumes nothing draws current from Vout. Anything you connect there is a **load**, and it sits in parallel with R2. That lowers the effective bottom resistance, so Vout falls.

```python
def par(a, b):
    return a * b / (a + b)

def divider(vin, r1, r2):
    return vin * r2 / (r1 + r2)

vin, r1, r2 = 3.3, 10e3, 10e3
v0 = divider(vin, r1, r2)
print(f"unloaded: {v0:.3f} V")
for load in (1e6, 100e3, 10e3, 1e3):
    v = divider(vin, r1, par(r2, load))
    k = load / 1e3
    print(f"load {k:>6.0f}k: {v:.3f} V")
```

```
unloaded: 1.650 V
load   1000k: 1.642 V
load    100k: 1.571 V
load     10k: 1.100 V
load      1k: 0.275 V
```

The rule of thumb is to make the load at least 10× (better 100×) the divider's resistances. A 1 MΩ load barely moves a 10 kΩ divider. A 10 kΩ load drags it from 1.65 V to 1.10 V.

The divider's **output resistance** (its source impedance) is R1 ∥ R2. Here that's 10 kΩ ∥ 10 kΩ = 5 kΩ. The lower it is, the less a load disturbs it, but the more standing current the divider wastes.

> [!note] Why this matters for ADCs
> A microcontroller's ADC input isn't a pure open circuit. Many ADCs briefly connect a small sampling capacitor that has to charge through the source's resistance. If the source impedance is too high, the reading comes out low or noisy. The chip's datasheet or reference manual states the maximum source impedance for a given sampling time. Check it for your board rather than assuming a value.

### Dividers are not power supplies

A divider can make a reference voltage for a high-impedance input. It can't power anything that draws significant or varying current. Feed a 5 V-to-3.3 V divider into a board's power pin and the voltage collapses as soon as the board draws current. Use a voltage regulator for power.

## The potentiometer: a divider with a moving tap

A **potentiometer** (pot) is a resistive track with a wiper that slides along it. It has three terminals: the two ends of the track and the wiper.

```diagram
  pin 1 ──/\/\/\/\/\/\── pin 3
              ↑
           pin 2 (wiper)
```

Wire one end to the supply, the other to ground, and the wiper is a divider output. Turn the knob and you move the split point between "R1" and "R2". The total stays fixed, so for a 10 kΩ pot, R1 + R2 = 10 kΩ at every position.

For a microcontroller knob:

```diagram
 3.3V ── pin 3
        pot track ── pin 2 ── ADC pin
 GND ── pin 1
```

Points to watch:

- **Use the board's documented analogue supply for the pot, matching the ADC range.** Do not load an unbuffered VREF pin unless the documentation explicitly allows it. If the pot is fed from a different voltage, the ADC's full range won't match the knob's full range. Feeding it from a higher voltage could also exceed the input's maximum (lesson 4).
- **Swapping pins 1 and 3** reverses the direction of the knob. It's harmless and easily fixed in software.
- **Never wire the wiper straight to a supply rail.** At one extreme the wiper sits at the end connected to ground, and you'd short the supply through a few ohms of track.
- **The pot's resistance** trades standing current against source impedance. Values around 10 kΩ are a common choice for microcontroller knobs, but confirm against the ADC's source-impedance limit.

## Linear and logarithmic (audio) taper

The **taper** (or law) is how resistance changes with rotation.

- **Linear taper:** halfway round, the wiper is at half the total resistance. Output voltage is proportional to angle.
- **Logarithmic or "audio" taper:** the resistance changes slowly at first, then quickly. A common specification is a 10% log taper, meaning the wiper is at 10% of the total at mid-rotation. Hearing is roughly logarithmic, so a log pot makes an analogue volume control feel even.

| Rotation | Linear | 10% log (approx.) |
|---|---|---|
| 0% | 0% | 0% |
| 50% | 50% | 10% |
| 100% | 100% | 100% |

Two practical warnings:

- **Markings aren't standardised.** Many Asian and US pots use "A" for log and "B" for linear, but some European makers use "A" for linear. Read the datasheet.
- **Cheap log pots are approximations,** often two linear segments joined near the middle.

> [!tip] For digital synths, usually choose linear
> When a pot feeds an ADC, you can apply any curve you like in software. A linear pot gives even resolution across the whole rotation, and code can map it to a logarithmic volume or exponential frequency response. A log pot is mostly useful when it directly controls an analogue audio level.

## Pitfalls

- **Forgetting the load.** A divider measured with nothing attached may read differently once connected.
- **Using a divider as a supply.** It can't hold its voltage under a changing load.
- **Pot fed from the wrong voltage.** Use the documented supply matched to the ADC range, never above the input's maximum.
- **Assuming the taper letter.** Check the datasheet.

## Key takeaways

- Series resistances add. Parallel resistances combine to less than the smallest branch; for two, (R1·R2)/(R1+R2).
- Vout = Vin × R2 / (R1 + R2). The ratio sets the voltage.
- A load sits in parallel with R2 and pulls Vout down. Keep loads well above the divider's resistance.
- The divider's output resistance is R1 ∥ R2. ADC inputs have a maximum source impedance; check the datasheet.
- A pot is a divider with a moving tap: ends to reference and ground, wiper to the ADC.
- Linear taper suits ADC knobs because curves can be applied in code. Log taper suits analogue volume.

questions.prompt: What is the combined resistance of a 4.7 kΩ resistor in series with a 2.2 kΩ resistor, and of the same two in parallel?

options.text: Series 6.9 kΩ, parallel about 1.5 kΩ
options.explanation: Correct. Series: 4.7 + 2.2 = 6.9 kΩ. Parallel: (4.7 × 2.2)/(4.7 + 2.2) = 10.34/6.9 ≈ 1.50 kΩ, smaller than the smaller resistor as it must be.

options.text: Series about 1.5 kΩ, parallel 6.9 kΩ
options.explanation: The formulas are swapped. Series adds, so the series total is the larger one.

options.text: Series 6.9 kΩ, parallel 3.45 kΩ
options.explanation: Halving the series total only works for two *equal* resistors. In general use (R1 × R2)/(R1 + R2).

options.text: Series 6.9 kΩ, parallel 2.5 kΩ
options.explanation: 2.5 kΩ is the difference (4.7 − 2.2). Parallel combination isn't subtraction.

questions.workedExample:
1. Series: R = R1 + R2 = 4.7 + 2.2 = 6.9 kΩ.
2. Parallel (two resistors): R = (R1 × R2) / (R1 + R2).
3. Numerator: 4.7 × 2.2 = 10.34 (kΩ²). Denominator: 6.9 kΩ.
4. 10.34 / 6.9 ≈ 1.50 kΩ.
5. Sanity check: the parallel result must be below 2.2 kΩ, the smallest branch. It is.

questions.prompt: An unloaded divider has R1 = 20 kΩ (top, to 5 V) and R2 = 10 kΩ (bottom, to ground). What is Vout?

options.explanation: That would need R1 = R2. Here the bottom resistor is only a third of the total.
This is Vin × R1/(R1 + R2), the voltage across the *top* resistor. Vout is across R2.

options.text: About 1.67 V

options.explanation: A resistive divider can never output more than its input. This is 5 × 20/10, an inverted ratio.

questions.workedExample:
1. Vout = Vin × R2 / (R1 + R2).
2. R2 / (R1 + R2) = 10 / 30 = 1/3.
3. Vout = 5 × 1/3 ≈ 1.67 V.
4. Check: the top resistor drops the other 3.33 V, and 1.67 + 3.33 = 5 V.

questions.prompt: A pot is wired with one end to 3.3 V, the other end to ground, and the wiper to an ADC pin. What does turning the knob change?

options.text: The total resistance between 3.3 V and ground
options.explanation: The track between the two ends is fixed. Only the wiper's position on it changes.

options.text: The ratio of the two parts of the track, and so the divider's output voltage
options.explanation: Correct. The wiper splits the fixed track into an upper part and a lower part. Their ratio sets the wiper voltage, from 0 V to 3.3 V.

options.text: The current drawn from the supply, from zero to maximum
options.explanation: The current through the track is 3.3 V / R_total, which is constant regardless of wiper position (ignoring the ADC's tiny load).

options.text: The ADC's reference voltage
options.explanation: The reference is fixed by the board. The pot produces a voltage between 0 V and its top end, which the ADC measures against that reference.

questions.workedExample:
1. The two ends of the track connect to 3.3 V and 0 V, so the full 10 kΩ (say) is always across the supply.
2. The wiper divides the track into R_top and R_bottom, with R_top + R_bottom = 10 kΩ.
3. Vwiper = 3.3 × R_bottom / 10 kΩ.
4. Rotating moves the split, so Vwiper sweeps from 0 V to 3.3 V while the supply current stays at 3.3 V / 10 kΩ = 0.33 mA.

questions.prompt: Two 10 kΩ resistors make a divider from 3.3 V (1.65 V unloaded). You connect a module whose input resistance is 10 kΩ to the output. What does Vout become?

options.text: Still 1.65 V, because the ratio of R1 to R2 hasn't changed
options.explanation: The load sits in parallel with R2 and changes the effective bottom resistance. The formula only holds unloaded.

options.text: About 2.2 V
options.explanation: The load lowers the bottom half, so Vout must fall, not rise.

options.text: 0.825 V, exactly half of the unloaded value
options.explanation: Halving the bottom resistance doesn't halve the output. Work it through: 3.3 × 5/(10 + 5).
Correct. R2 ∥ 10 kΩ = 5 kΩ, so Vout = 3.3 × 5/(10 + 5) = 1.1 V.

questions.workedExample:
1. The load is in parallel with R2: 10 kΩ ∥ 10 kΩ = 5 kΩ.
2. New divider: R1 = 10 kΩ, effective R2 = 5 kΩ.
3. Vout = 3.3 × 5 / (10 + 5) = 3.3 / 3 = 1.1 V.
4. The output fell by a third. A load comparable to the divider's own resistance is far too heavy. Aim for 10× to 100× larger.

questions.prompt: What is the output (source) resistance of a divider made from R1 = 10 kΩ and R2 = 10 kΩ, as seen by whatever connects to Vout?

options.text: 20 kΩ
options.explanation: That's the series total between the supply and ground, which sets the standing current, not the output resistance.

options.text: 5 kΩ
options.explanation: Correct. Looking back into Vout, the supply acts as a short for small changes, so R1 and R2 appear in parallel: 10 ∥ 10 = 5 kΩ.

options.text: 10 kΩ
options.explanation: That counts only R2. R1 also connects Vout to a fixed voltage (the supply), so it appears in parallel with R2.

options.text: 0 Ω, because the supply is ideal
options.explanation: An ideal supply has zero resistance, but it connects through R1, so the output still sees R1 ∥ R2.

questions.workedExample:
1. Thevenin view: replace the supply with its internal resistance (≈ 0 Ω for an ideal supply).
2. From Vout, R1 now goes to ground through the supply and R2 goes straight to ground.
3. They're in parallel: R_out = R1 ∥ R2 = (10 × 10)/(10 + 10) = 5 kΩ.
4. Use it as a rule: a load much larger than R_out barely disturbs the divider, and a load comparable to R_out pulls the output well down.

questions.prompt: You want to run a 3.3 V board from a 5 V USB supply, so you build a divider from 1 kΩ and 2 kΩ and feed its output into the board's 3.3 V power pin. What happens?

options.text: The voltage collapses well below 3.3 V as soon as the board draws current, and varies with its load. Use a regulator instead
options.explanation: Correct. A divider's output depends on the load. A board drawing, say, 100 mA through a 1 kΩ top resistor would need a 100 V drop, which is impossible, so the output falls nearly to zero.

options.text: It works: 5 × 2/3 = 3.33 V
options.explanation: That's the unloaded voltage. The board draws tens to hundreds of milliamps, which is a very heavy, varying load in parallel with the 2 kΩ.

options.text: The voltage rises above 3.3 V and damages the board
options.explanation: Adding a load can only *lower* a divider's output. The danger with a divider supply is collapse, not overvoltage. Even so, never feed a power pin from an unregulated source of unknown voltage.

options.text: It works if you use 10 kΩ and 20 kΩ instead to save power
options.explanation: Higher resistances make the output *weaker*. With 10 kΩ on top, the board could draw only a fraction of a milliamp before the voltage collapses.

questions.workedExample:
1. Unloaded: 5 × 2/(1 + 2) = 3.33 V. It looks right on a meter with nothing attached.
2. The board is a load, perhaps 100 mA, equivalent to roughly 33 Ω at 3.3 V.
3. 2 kΩ ∥ 33 Ω ≈ 32.5 Ω. Vout ≈ 5 × 32.5/(1000 + 32.5) ≈ 0.16 V.
4. The board won't run, and as its current changes so does the voltage.
5. A regulator actively holds its output constant as load current changes. That's the right part for power.

questions.prompt: A pot marked "B10K" arrives from a supplier. What can you safely conclude?

options.text: It is 10 kΩ and certainly linear
options.explanation: "B" commonly means linear on Asian and US parts, but the letters aren't standardised. Some European makers use other letter schemes.

options.text: It is 10 kΩ log, because B stands for "bass"
options.explanation: There's no such convention. Taper codes vary by maker; "B" is often linear.

options.text: It is 10 kΩ, and the taper letter suggests linear on many parts but should be confirmed in the datasheet or by measuring
options.explanation: Correct. 10K is the track resistance. The taper letter convention varies between manufacturers, so check the datasheet, or measure the wiper resistance at mid-rotation (about 5 kΩ for linear, about 1 kΩ for a 10% log).

options.text: It is a 10 kΩ fixed resistor
options.explanation: "K" is the kilohm multiplier. The letter in front is the taper code of a potentiometer.

questions.workedExample:
1. "10K" gives the end-to-end track resistance: 10 kΩ.
2. The taper letter isn't standardised. A/B/C have different meanings between regions and makers.
3. Confirm: set the knob to mid-rotation and measure from one end to the wiper, with the pot out of circuit (unpowered).
   - About 5 kΩ means linear.
   - About 1 kΩ (or 9 kΩ from the other end) means a 10% log taper.

questions.prompt: Which of these are reasons to choose a *linear* pot for a knob read by a microcontroller ADC? Select all that apply.

options.text: You can apply any response curve in software after reading it
options.explanation: Correct. Code can map the reading to an exponential frequency or logarithmic level curve.

options.text: It spreads the ADC's resolution evenly across the rotation
options.explanation: Correct. With a log pot, much of the rotation is squeezed into a small part of the ADC range, wasting codes at one end.

options.text: Log pots can't be connected to ADCs
options.explanation: A log pot works electrically. It's just a divider with a non-linear track. The point is that it's usually unnecessary.

options.text: Linear pots have lower noise than log pots in all cases
options.explanation: There's no general rule that taper decides noise. This isn't a reason taught in the lesson.

questions.workedExample:
1. The ADC converts voltage to a number. Any curve after that is arithmetic.
2. Linear pot: equal rotation gives equal ADC codes, so resolution is even everywhere.
3. 10% log pot: the first half of the rotation covers only 10% of the voltage range, so it gets about a tenth of the codes. That's coarse at the start.
4. Log pots are still useful when the pot directly sets an analogue audio level with no software in between.

questions.prompt: Your ADC's datasheet limits the source impedance to a few kilohms for the sampling time you've chosen. You're reading a 100 kΩ linear pot wired as a divider. At what wiper position is its source impedance highest, and what is it?

options.text: At either end, 100 kΩ
options.explanation: At the ends one part of the track is 0 Ω, so the source impedance is about 0 Ω, its lowest.

options.text: At mid-rotation, 50 kΩ
options.explanation: 50 kΩ is each half, but the two halves are in parallel as seen from the wiper, which gives 25 kΩ.

options.text: It's constant at 100 kΩ
options.explanation: The end-to-end resistance is constant, but the impedance seen at the wiper depends on position.

options.text: At mid-rotation, 25 kΩ
options.explanation: Correct. Source impedance is R_top ∥ R_bottom. At mid-rotation that's 50 k ∥ 50 k = 25 kΩ, the maximum, and well above a few kilohms.

questions.workedExample:
1. A pot wired as a divider has source impedance R_top ∥ R_bottom, with R_top + R_bottom = R.
2. With x = fraction of R below the wiper: Z = R·x·(1 − x).
3. This peaks at x = 0.5: Z = R/4 = 100/4 = 25 kΩ.
4. At the ends (x = 0 or 1) Z ≈ 0.
5. Fixes: use a lower-value pot (10 kΩ peaks at 2.5 kΩ), lengthen the sampling time, or add a small capacitor or buffer at the ADC pin, checking your chip's documentation for which is recommended.

questions.prompt: A divider must give about 1.0 V from 3.3 V for a reference input whose input resistance is around 1 MΩ. Which choice is best, and why?

options.text: R1 = 2.3 Ω, R2 = 1 Ω: lowest output resistance
options.explanation: The ratio is right, but 3.3 V across 3.3 Ω draws 1 A and wastes 3.3 W. That's absurd for a reference.

options.text: R1 = 2.3 MΩ, R2 = 1 MΩ: lowest power
options.explanation: The power is tiny, but the 1 MΩ load is now in parallel with the 1 MΩ R2, halving it. The output falls to about 0.59 V.

options.text: R1 = 23 kΩ, R2 = 10 kΩ: right ratio, the 1 MΩ load is about 140× the ~7 kΩ output resistance, and the standing current is only 0.1 mA
options.explanation: Correct. Vout = 3.3 × 10/33 = 1.0 V. R_out = 23 k ∥ 10 k ≈ 7 kΩ, so the 1 MΩ load shifts the output by under 1%. Standing current = 3.3/33 k = 0.1 mA.

options.text: Any pair with a 2.3:1 ratio works equally well
options.explanation: Only for an unloaded divider. With a real load, absolute values decide how much the output sags and how much power is wasted.

questions.workedExample:
1. Ratio: Vout/Vin = 1.0/3.3 ≈ 0.303, so R2/(R1 + R2) ≈ 0.303 and R1 ≈ 2.3 × R2.
2. Check loading for each option.
   - 23 k/10 k: R_out = (23 × 10)/33 ≈ 7.0 kΩ. 1 MΩ ∥ 10 kΩ = 9.90 kΩ, so Vout = 3.3 × 9.90/32.9 ≈ 0.993 V. Fine.
   - 2.3 M/1 M: 1 MΩ ∥ 1 MΩ = 500 kΩ, so Vout = 3.3 × 0.5/2.8 ≈ 0.59 V. Badly loaded.
3. Check power: 23 k + 10 k draws 0.1 mA (0.33 mW). The 3.3 Ω pair draws 1 A.
4. Middle values balance loading against waste.

questions.prompt: Which statements about wiring a pot to a microcontroller are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Swapping the two end pins reverses the knob's direction but is otherwise harmless
options.explanation: Correct. It mirrors the divider, and you can invert it in software if you prefer.

options.text: Connecting the wiper directly to 3.3 V and one end to ground risks shorting the supply when the knob is at that end
options.explanation: Correct. At that extreme the wiper sits on the grounded end, connecting 3.3 V to ground through almost zero track resistance.

options.text: The top of the pot should normally be the ADC's reference voltage, and never above the pin's maximum input
options.explanation: Correct. This maps the full rotation onto the full ADC range and keeps the pin within its rating (on Teensy 4.1, for example, analogue pins aren't 5 V tolerant).

options.text: Feeding the pot from 5 V gives better resolution on a 3.3 V ADC
options.explanation: The ADC can't measure above its reference, and on 3.3 V-only pins 5 V can damage the chip. It loses part of the range and risks damage.

questions.workedExample:
1. End pins: the divider is symmetric, so swapping reverses direction only.
2. Wiper to a rail: at full rotation one end-to-wiper segment is ~0 Ω. With that end at ground and the wiper on 3.3 V, the supply is shorted.
3. Reference: if the ADC measures 0 to 3.3 V, the pot should span 0 to 3.3 V. Teensy 4.1's documentation (PJRC, checked 4 Oct 2026) says its analogue range is fixed at 0 to 3.3 V and the pins aren't 5 V tolerant. Check your own board.
4. 5 V feed: above 66% of the ideal linear pot's voltage travel from ground the pin would see more than 3.3 V, outside its rating.

lessons.title: Components: resistors, capacitors, LEDs, diodes, switches and connectors
lessons.summary: The parts in every synth build. How to read their values and ratings, size an LED resistor, use the RC time constant, respect polarity, and check connector pinouts.
lessons.body:
A synth build uses a small set of passive parts over and over. Each one has a **value** (what it does) and **ratings** (what it survives). Most beginner damage comes from ignoring the ratings or the polarity, not from getting the value slightly wrong.

## Resistors

### Reading the value

Through-hole resistors use colour bands defined by IEC 60062. Read from the end where the bands bunch together. The gold or silver tolerance band is usually at the other end, often slightly separated.

| Colour | Digit | Multiplier |
|---|---|---|
| Black | 0 | ×1 |
| Brown | 1 | ×10 |
| Red | 2 | ×100 |
| Orange | 3 | ×1k |
| Yellow | 4 | ×10k |
| Green | 5 | ×100k |
| Blue | 6 | ×1M |
| Violet | 7 | ×10M |
| Grey | 8 | ×100M |
| White | 9 | ×1G |
| Gold | | ×0.1 |
| Silver | | ×0.01 |

- **Four-band:** digit, digit, multiplier, tolerance. Yellow-violet-red-gold = 4, 7, ×100 = 4.7 kΩ ±5%.
- **Five-band** (precision): digit, digit, digit, multiplier, tolerance. Brown-black-black-red-brown = 1, 0, 0, ×100 = 10 kΩ ±1%.
- **Tolerance band:** brown ±1%, red ±2%, gold ±5%, silver ±10%.

Colours are easy to misread under poor light. Brown, red and orange look alike, and so do violet and grey. **Measure with a multimeter before fitting** (out of circuit) whenever you're unsure.

### Preferred values

Resistors come in E-series values. E12 (for ±10%) has 12 values per decade: 10, 12, 15, 18, 22, 27, 33, 39, 47, 56, 68, 82. E24 adds more in between. You calculate an ideal value, then choose the nearest standard value in the safe direction.

### Tolerance and power rating

- **Tolerance:** a 10 kΩ ±5% part may be anywhere from 9.5 to 10.5 kΩ. For a divider that sets a precise level, use 1% parts.
- **Power rating:** common small through-hole resistors are rated around 0.25 W. Check the datasheet. Calculate P = I²R and leave margin. Running at half the rating or less is a common conservative practice.

## Capacitors

A capacitor stores charge between two plates separated by an insulator (the dielectric). Capacitance C is measured in farads (F). Practical values run from pF to thousands of µF.

### Behaviour

- It **blocks steady DC** once charged, because no current flows through the insulator.
- It **passes changes**, since current flows while its voltage is changing. This is why it can remove a DC offset from an audio signal or short fast noise to ground.
- Its voltage **can't jump instantly**. It changes at a rate set by the current.

### The RC time constant

Charge a capacitor C through a resistor R from a fixed voltage and it follows an exponential curve. The **time constant** is:

```
τ = R × C      (ohms × farads = seconds)
```

After one τ the capacitor reaches about 63.2% of the applied voltage. After 5τ it's within 1% of it.

```python
import math

tau = 10e3 * 100e-9    # 10 kΩ, 100 nF
for n in (1, 2, 3, 5):
    pct = 100 * (1 - math.exp(-n))
    ms = n * tau * 1e3
    t = f"{n} tau = {ms:.1f} ms"
    print(f"{t}: {pct:.1f}%")
```

```
1 tau = 1.0 ms: 63.2%
2 tau = 2.0 ms: 86.5%
3 tau = 3.0 ms: 95.0%
5 tau = 5.0 ms: 99.3%
```

RC circuits show up across synth hardware. They give a simple low-pass filter (its −3 dB cutoff is f = 1 / (2πRC)). They smooth a noisy knob, and they slow a bouncing switch.

### Types

| Type | Polarised? | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| Ceramic (MLCC) | No | Decoupling (100 nF), small values |
| Film | No | Audio signal paths, filters |
| Aluminium electrolytic | **Yes** | Bulk supply filtering, large µF |
| Tantalum | **Yes** | Compact bulk capacitance |

Things to watch:

- **Polarity.** Electrolytic and tantalum capacitors must have their + lead at the higher voltage. On aluminium electrolytics a stripe marks the **negative** lead, and the negative lead is usually the shorter one. On tantalum capacitors the marking works the other way: a stripe or bar usually marks the **positive** lead. Check the datasheet. Reverse them and they can overheat, vent or burst; tantalums can fail short and catch fire. Don't use a polarised capacitor where the voltage across it can reverse, such as a plain AC audio signal with no DC bias.
- **Voltage rating.** Every capacitor has a maximum working voltage. Choose one comfortably above the highest voltage it will see. A 6.3 V capacitor on a 5 V rail leaves little margin, so 10 V or 16 V is more comfortable. Margin is a design rule of thumb; check the manufacturer's guidance for the part.
- **Ceramic DC bias.** Many high-value ceramics (X7R, X5R and similar Class 2 dielectrics) lose a significant share of their capacitance when a DC voltage is applied, sometimes well over half near the rated voltage. The effect is documented in manufacturers' DC-bias curves. The "X7R" code itself only describes temperature behaviour (±15% from −55 to +125 °C); it says nothing about voltage. C0G/NP0 ceramics are stable but only come in small values.
- **Markings.** Small ceramics often use three digits: `104` = 10 × 10⁴ pF = 100 nF.

## LEDs and the current-limiting resistor

An LED is a diode that emits light. It conducts in one direction only. Above its **forward voltage** V_f the current rises very steeply, so an LED always needs something to limit its current, usually a series resistor.

V_f depends on colour and current. For a typical red indicator LED it's around 1.8–2.2 V at 20 mA, and for blue and white around 3–3.5 V. Datasheet maximums are higher: Kingbright's 5 mm parts, for example, list a red at 1.85 V typical, 2.5 V maximum, and a blue at 3.3 V typical, 4.0 V maximum. Use the figures from your LED's datasheet. Small 3 mm and 5 mm indicator LEDs are usually characterised at 20 mA, with an absolute-maximum continuous current often in the 20–30 mA range. Treat 20 mA as a ceiling, not a target: they're usually bright enough at a few milliamps.

```
R = (V_supply − V_f) / I_LED
```

```python
import math

def led_resistor(vs, vf, i):
    return (vs - vf) / i

E12 = [10, 12, 15, 18, 22, 27,
       33, 39, 47, 56, 68, 82]

def next_e12_up(r):
    dec = 10 ** math.floor(math.log10(r))
    for base in E12 + [100]:
        if base * dec / 10 >= r:
            return base * dec / 10

r = led_resistor(3.3, 2.0, 0.005)
pick = next_e12_up(r)
i = (3.3 - 2.0) / pick
print(f"ideal R = {r:.0f} ohm")
print(f"E12 pick = {pick:.0f} ohm")
print(f"actual I = {i*1000:.2f} mA")
```

```
ideal R = 260 ohm
E12 pick = 270 ohm
actual I = 4.81 mA
```

Round **up** to the next standard value. That gives slightly less current, which is the safe direction. Then check the resistor's power, (1.3 V × 4.8 mA ≈ 6 mW), and the source's limits. When a microcontroller pin drives the LED, the pin's maximum output current from the board's datasheet also applies.

**LED polarity:** the longer leg is usually the anode (+). The cathode (−) is often marked by a flat on the rim. Check the datasheet. Reversed, it just stays dark at these voltages, but don't rely on reverse-voltage tolerance. LED reverse ratings are often only a few volts.

## Diodes

A diode lets conventional current flow from **anode** to **cathode** (towards the bar in its schematic symbol; an LED's outward arrows represent emitted light) and blocks it the other way. The cathode is marked with a band.

| Type | Forward drop (approx.) | Common use |
|---|---|---|
| Silicon (e.g. 1N4148) | ~0.6–0.75 V at a few mA | Small-signal, clamping |
| Silicon rectifier (e.g. 1N400x) | ~0.7 V small current, up to ~1 V at 1 A | Reverse-polarity protection |
| Schottky | ~0.2–0.4 V small current, ~0.45–0.6 V at 1 A | Low-drop protection |

The forward drops are approximate, and they rise with current and fall with temperature. Datasheets guarantee a maximum at a stated current (the 1N4148's is 1 V at 10 mA; the 1N5817 Schottky's is 0.45 V at 1 A) and show the typical curve.

Uses in a synth:

- **Reverse-polarity protection:** a series diode in the supply line blocks current if the supply is connected backwards, at the cost of its forward drop.
- **Clamping:** diodes to the supply rails catch input overvoltage (lesson 4).
- **Flyback:** a diode across a relay or motor coil absorbs the voltage spike when the coil switches off.

## Switches and buttons

Switches are described by **poles** (independent circuits switched) and **throws** (positions each pole can connect to):

- **SPST:** single pole, single throw. A simple on/off.
- **SPDT:** single pole, double throw. A common terminal switches between two others.
- **DPDT:** two SPDT switches moved together.

**Momentary** buttons only connect while pressed. **Latching** (toggle) switches stay put. Tactile buttons often have four legs that are internally connected in pairs. Check which pairs with a continuity tester before wiring.

Mechanical contacts **bounce**: for a few milliseconds a press looks like several rapid presses. A microcontroller reading a button also needs a defined idle level from a pull-up or pull-down resistor. Debouncing and pull-ups are covered with the embedded topics.

## Connectors and pinouts

Connectors are where parts are most often wired wrong.

- **Pin headers** are commonly on a 2.54 mm (0.1 in) pitch. Pin 1 is marked by a square pad, a triangle or a dot.
- **Pinout diagrams can be drawn from either side.** "Looking into the socket" and "looking at the solder side" are mirror images. Check which view the diagram shows.
- **Audio jacks:** on a 3.5 mm or 6.35 mm TRS stereo jack, tip = left, ring = right, sleeve = ground. On a mono TS jack, tip = signal and sleeve = ground.
- **Keying:** keyed connectors only fit one way. Unkeyed headers fit both ways, including the wrong one.
- **Product-specific connectors** (power inputs, MIDI DIN, board edge headers) have pinouts defined by the product or standard. Take them from that documentation, never from memory. DIN MIDI isn't a direct GPIO connection; it needs the interface circuit from the MIDI specification, covered in a later module.

> [!warning] Polarity and pinout mistakes destroy parts
> Before power-up, check every polarised part (electrolytics, diodes, LEDs, chips) and every connector orientation against the schematic. It takes a minute and catches the most common fatal mistakes.

## Key takeaways

- Read resistor bands from the bunched end. Brown-red-gold-silver tolerance is 1%, 2%, 5%, 10%. Measure when unsure.
- Choose standard E-series values. Check power with P = I²R and leave margin.
- τ = RC: 63.2% after one τ, about 99% after 5τ.
- Electrolytic and tantalum capacitors are polarised. Respect polarity and choose a voltage rating with margin.
- LED resistor: R = (V_supply − V_f) / I, rounded up. Respect pin and LED current limits.
- Diodes conduct anode to cathode (banded end) with a forward drop of roughly 0.6–0.7 V for silicon at small currents, rising towards 1 V at amps.
- Switch types: poles and throws, momentary or latching. Contacts bounce.
- Take pinouts from documentation and note which side the diagram is drawn from.

## Further reading

- [Electronic color code, IEC 60062 (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_color_code)
- [E series of preferred numbers (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E_series_of_preferred_numbers)
- [RC time constant (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RC_time_constant)
- [Electrolytic capacitor: polarity and failure (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrolytic_capacitor)
- [Ceramic capacitor, including voltage dependence (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceramic_capacitor)
- [Diode (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diode)
- [Light-emitting diodes (SparkFun)](https://learn.sparkfun.com/tutorials/light-emitting-diodes-leds/all)
- [Phone connector (audio): TRS wiring (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phone_connector_(audio))
- [Flyback diode (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flyback_diode)

questions.prompt: A four-band resistor reads yellow, violet, orange, gold. What is it?

options.explanation: That would need a red (×100) multiplier. Orange is ×1000.
Correct. Yellow = 4, violet = 7, orange = ×1000, so 47 × 1000 = 47 kΩ. Gold = ±5%.
On a four-band resistor the third band is the multiplier, not a third digit.
Gold is ±5%. Silver is ±10%.

questions.workedExample:
1. Start from the end where the bands bunch up; the gold band is at the far end.
2. Band 1 yellow = 4, band 2 violet = 7, giving 47.
3. Band 3 orange is the multiplier, ×10³.
4. 47 × 1000 = 47,000 Ω = 47 kΩ.
5. Band 4 gold = ±5%, so 44.65 kΩ to 49.35 kΩ.
6. If you're unsure of the colours, measure it out of circuit.

questions.prompt: An aluminium electrolytic capacitor has a stripe with minus signs down one side. Which lead goes to the more positive voltage?

options.text: The lead under the stripe
options.explanation: The stripe marks the *negative* lead on aluminium electrolytics. Putting it at the higher voltage reverses the capacitor.

options.text: Either: capacitors aren't polarised
options.explanation: Ceramic and film capacitors aren't polarised, but electrolytics are. Reverse voltage can overheat or burst them.

options.text: The lead away from the stripe, usually the longer one
options.explanation: Correct. The stripe marks the negative lead (usually the shorter one), so the other lead is positive.

options.text: The shorter lead
options.explanation: On a new electrolytic the shorter lead is usually the negative one, the same lead the stripe marks.

questions.workedExample:
1. Aluminium electrolytics are polarised: + must sit at the higher voltage.
2. Markings: a stripe (often with − signs) marks the negative lead, which is usually also the shorter lead.
3. So the unmarked, longer lead is positive.
4. Always confirm against the schematic's + symbol before soldering. A reversed electrolytic can vent or burst.

questions.prompt: A 10 kΩ resistor charges a 1 µF capacitor from 0 V towards 5 V. What is the time constant, and roughly what is the capacitor voltage after one time constant?

options.text: 10 ms, about 3.2 V
options.explanation: Correct. τ = RC = 10,000 × 0.000001 = 0.01 s = 10 ms. After one τ the voltage reaches about 63.2% of 5 V ≈ 3.16 V.
After one τ the voltage is 63.2% of the final value, not 50%.

options.text: 10 s, about 3.2 V
options.explanation: Prefix slip. 1 µF is 10⁻⁶ F, so RC = 10⁴ × 10⁻⁶ = 10⁻² s.

options.text: 10 ms, 5 V
options.explanation: A capacitor only gets close to the full voltage after about 5τ (≈ 99%), not after 1τ.

questions.prompt: You want about 5 mA through a blue LED from a 5 V supply. Its datasheet gives V_f ≈ 3.0 V. Using E12 values (… 330, 390, 470, 560 …), rounding upward to keep the nominal current at or below 5 mA, which resistor do you choose, and what current results?

options.text: 390 Ω, about 5.1 mA
options.explanation: 390 Ω is the nearest value *below* the ideal 400 Ω, so the current comes out slightly over target. Rounding up is the safe direction.

options.text: 1 kΩ, about 2 mA
options.explanation: That works and is safe, but it isn't the closest standard value above 400 Ω. 470 Ω gets nearer the target.

options.text: 470 Ω, about 4.3 mA
options.explanation: Correct. Ideal R = (5 − 3)/0.005 = 400 Ω. The next E12 value up is 470 Ω, giving 2/470 ≈ 4.3 mA.

options.text: 1 kΩ, because 5 V / 5 mA = 1 kΩ
options.explanation: This ignores the LED's 3 V forward drop. Only 2 V is across the resistor.

questions.workedExample:
1. Voltage across the resistor: 5.0 − 3.0 = 2.0 V.
2. Ideal R = 2.0 / 0.005 = 400 Ω.
3. E12 neighbours: 390 Ω (below) and 470 Ω (above). Round up so the current falls slightly rather than exceeding the target.
4. Actual I = 2.0 / 470 ≈ 4.26 mA.
5. Power: 2.0 × 0.00426 ≈ 8.5 mW, trivial for a 0.25 W part.

questions.prompt: A 5 V rail needs a bulk electrolytic capacitor. Which voltage rating is the most sensible choice?

options.text: 4 V
options.explanation: That's below the rail voltage. The capacitor would be over-stressed from the start.

options.text: 5 V, exactly matching the rail
options.explanation: With no margin, any ripple or spike above 5 V exceeds the rating.
Technically above 5 V, but with little margin for spikes and tolerance. It's a common rating, but more margin is the conservative choice.

options.text: 10 V or 16 V
options.explanation: Correct. A rating comfortably above the highest voltage the capacitor will see gives margin against spikes and improves reliability. Check the manufacturer's derating guidance.

questions.workedExample:
1. The working voltage rating is a maximum, not a target.
2. Real rails carry ripple and switching spikes, and plugging and unplugging can cause brief overshoots.
3. A rating at or barely above the rail leaves no margin.
4. Choosing 10 V or 16 V for a 5 V rail is a common, conservative choice. The size and cost penalty is small.

questions.prompt: Which statements about polarity are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: An LED's longer leg is usually the anode (+)
options.explanation: Correct. It's the usual convention, though a datasheet or a quick test with a meter's diode mode confirms it.

options.text: The band on a diode marks the cathode
options.explanation: Correct. Conventional current flows from anode to the banded cathode when the diode is forward biased.

options.text: Ceramic 100 nF decoupling capacitors must be fitted with the right polarity
options.explanation: Ceramic capacitors aren't polarised; either orientation works.

options.text: A tantalum capacitor can be fitted either way round
options.explanation: Tantalum capacitors are polarised, like aluminium electrolytics. Reverse voltage can cause failure.

questions.workedExample:
Go through the parts:

- LED: polarised; long leg usually the anode, flat rim on the cathode side. True.
- Diode: band = cathode. True.
- Ceramic (MLCC): not polarised. False.
- Tantalum: polarised. False.

Rule: before power-up, check every polarised part against the schematic.

questions.prompt: A front-panel switch needs to route a signal to either output A or output B. Which switch type does that with one moving contact?

options.text: SPST
options.explanation: Single throw means only on/off on one path. It can't choose between two destinations.

options.text: SPDT
options.explanation: Correct. Single pole, double throw: one common terminal connects to one of two others.

options.text: DPST
options.explanation: Double pole, single throw switches two separate circuits on and off together. It still has no second position to route to.

options.text: A momentary push button
options.explanation: Momentary refers to spring return, not routing. A typical momentary button is SPST.

questions.workedExample:
1. Poles = independent circuits switched; throws = positions each pole can connect to.
2. You need one circuit (one pole) choosing between two destinations (two throws).
3. That's SPDT: the common terminal connects to A in one position and B in the other.
4. For stereo (two signals switched together) you'd use DPDT.

questions.prompt: Which statements about connectors and pinouts are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: On a TRS stereo jack, tip = left, ring = right, sleeve = ground
options.explanation: Correct. That's the standard stereo convention.

options.text: A pinout drawn "looking into the socket" is a mirror image of one drawn from the solder side
options.explanation: Correct. Always check which view a diagram uses before soldering.

options.text: An unkeyed 2.54 mm header can only be plugged in the correct way
options.explanation: Unkeyed headers fit either way round, including the wrong one. Mark pin 1 on both halves.

options.text: DIN MIDI can be wired straight to any microcontroller GPIO pin
options.explanation: DIN MIDI needs the interface circuit from the MIDI specification. It isn't a direct GPIO connection.

questions.workedExample:
1. TRS: tip/ring/sleeve = left/right/ground for stereo audio. True.
2. Views: a connector seen from the front and from the back are mirror images, so pin numbering appears reversed. True.
3. Unkeyed headers can be reversed. False.
4. DIN MIDI needs a documented interface circuit. False.

questions.prompt: You wire a four-legged tactile button between a GPIO pin and ground. The input reads "pressed" all the time, even with nothing touched. What's the most likely cause?

options.text: The button is faulty out of the box
options.explanation: Possible but unlikely. The usual cause is wiring, and you should check that first.

options.text: The button bounces
options.explanation: Bounce lasts milliseconds after a press. It doesn't make the input read pressed permanently.

options.text: Buttons need a capacitor to work
options.explanation: A capacitor can help with debouncing, but its absence doesn't make the button read pressed all the time.

options.text: You used two legs that are internally connected, so the pin is permanently shorted to ground
options.explanation: Correct. Tactile buttons usually have two pairs of legs joined internally. Wiring across a joined pair makes a permanent connection. Use legs from different pairs, and confirm with a continuity test.

questions.workedExample:
1. A four-leg tactile switch has two contacts, each reached through a pair of legs joined inside the package.
2. If both wires go to the same internal pair, the pin connects to ground whatever the button does.
3. Diagnose with power off: continuity between the two legs you used, button released. A beep confirms they're joined.
4. Fix: move one wire to a leg from the other pair, usually the diagonally opposite leg. Then confirm continuity only when pressed.

questions.prompt: A board's datasheet says each GPIO pin should source no more than 4 mA. You drive a red LED (V_f ≈ 2.0 V) from a 3.3 V pin through 150 Ω. Is that acceptable, and if not, using the stated nominal voltages and ignoring tolerances, what is the smallest E12 resistor (… 270, 330, 390 …) that keeps within 4 mA?

options.text: Acceptable: 150 Ω gives about 4 mA
options.explanation: 1.3 V / 150 Ω ≈ 8.7 mA, more than twice the limit.

options.text: Not acceptable: about 8.7 mA flows. The minimum is 1.3 V / 4 mA = 325 Ω, so use 330 Ω (≈ 3.9 mA)
options.explanation: Correct. Calculate the current, compare with the pin limit, then size the resistor to the limit and round up to a standard value.

options.text: Not acceptable; use 270 Ω
options.explanation: 270 Ω gives 1.3/270 ≈ 4.8 mA, still above 4 mA. Round up to 330 Ω, not down.

options.text: Acceptable, because the LED limits its own current
options.explanation: An LED doesn't regulate its own current. Above V_f the current rises steeply, so the resistor has to set it.

questions.workedExample:
1. Current now: (3.3 − 2.0) / 150 = 1.3 / 150 ≈ 8.7 mA, over the 4 mA limit.
2. Minimum resistance for 4 mA: 1.3 / 0.004 = 325 Ω.
3. Round up to the next E12 value: 330 Ω.
4. New current: 1.3 / 330 ≈ 3.9 mA, within the limit.
5. Also check the datasheet's total-current limit for all pins together if many LEDs are lit.

This is a nominal calculation, not a worst-case guarantee. For hardware choose using maximum supply, minimum LED forward voltage and minimum resistor tolerance; 330 Ω may not leave enough margin.

questions.prompt: You fit a 10 µF X7R ceramic capacitor rated at 6.3 V on a 5 V rail. In circuit, its effective capacitance is far below 10 µF. Why?

options.text: Ceramic capacitors lose capacitance only from age, not from voltage
options.explanation: Ageing is real for Class 2 ceramics, but the dominant effect here is the applied DC voltage.

options.text: It was fitted backwards, so it's acting as a smaller capacitor
options.explanation: Ceramic capacitors aren't polarised. Orientation doesn't change their capacitance.

options.text: Class 2 ceramics such as X7R lose a substantial share of their capacitance under DC bias, especially near their rated voltage
options.explanation: Correct. The manufacturer's DC-bias curve shows how much remains at your operating voltage. Using a higher-voltage rating or a larger case size usually helps.

options.text: The 10 µF marking means 10 µF at 5 V exactly
options.explanation: The nominal value is measured with little or no DC bias. Under bias, Class 2 ceramics read lower.

questions.workedExample:
1. X7R, X5R and similar Class 2 ceramics use ferroelectric dielectrics whose permittivity falls as DC field strength rises.
2. At 5 V on a 6.3 V part, the field is high, so the effective capacitance can drop dramatically. Read the manufacturer's DC-bias curve for the exact figure.
3. Remedies: a higher voltage rating, a larger package, or a C0G/NP0 or electrolytic part where appropriate.
4. Lesson: the nominal value is a starting point. Check the datasheet curves for real operating conditions.

questions.prompt: An RC low-pass filter uses R = 10 kΩ and C = 10 nF. Approximately where is its −3 dB cutoff frequency?

options.text: About 1.6 kHz
About 10 kHz
options.explanation: That's 1/(RC) = 10,000 rad/s mistaken for hertz. The formula divides by 2π as well.

options.text: About 100 Hz
options.explanation: Prefix slip: this treats 10 nF as about 160 nF. 10 nF = 10⁻⁸ F.

options.text: About 16 kHz
options.explanation: Off by ten. Recheck the exponent: RC = 10⁴ × 10⁻⁸ = 10⁻⁴ s.

questions.workedExample:
1. RC = 10,000 Ω × 10 × 10⁻⁹ F = 10⁻⁴ s (τ = 0.1 ms).
2. f_c = 1 / (2π × RC) = 1 / (6.283 × 10⁻⁴).
3. f_c ≈ 1592 Hz ≈ 1.6 kHz.

This is the same circuit that smooths a noisy knob reading. Larger RC means a lower cutoff and more smoothing, but a slower response.

lessons.title: Power, logic levels and datasheets
lessons.summary: 3.3 V versus 5 V, logic thresholds and noise margins, absolute maximum ratings versus recommended operating conditions, how to read a datasheet, protecting inputs, and why every chip needs a decoupling capacitor.
lessons.body:
The fastest way to destroy a microcontroller board is to connect something at the wrong voltage. This lesson covers how to know, from the documents, what each pin will accept, and how to make two parts with different supplies talk safely.

> [!warning] Scope
> Everything here concerns low-voltage DC logic and audio circuits, typically 3.3 V and 5 V. Power your circuits from a certified USB supply or bench supply. Mains power-supply design is out of scope.

## Supply voltages: 3.3 V and 5 V

Two supply voltages dominate hobby digital electronics:

- **5 V:** USB's supply voltage, and the native supply of older logic families and many classic microcontrollers.
- **3.3 V:** the supply of most modern microcontrollers, including the ARM chips on audio-focused boards.

Many boards accept 5 V from USB and use an on-board **regulator** to make 3.3 V for the chip. The board may expose both voltages on pins. **The fact that 5 V exists on the board says nothing about whether the chip's I/O pins tolerate 5 V.**

> [!example] A real board's limits
> PJRC's Teensy 4.1 page (checked 4 October 2026) states that its digital pins accept 0 to 3.3 V signals and "are not 5V tolerant", and that the analogue range is fixed at 0 to 3.3 V. Other boards differ: some microcontrollers have individual 5 V-tolerant pins. Read the exact board and revision's documentation and the microcontroller datasheet, and record the date you checked.

## Logic levels and thresholds

A digital input doesn't care about the exact voltage. It decides "high" or "low" using thresholds from its datasheet:

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| V_IH(min) | Lowest voltage guaranteed read as high |
| V_IL(max) | Highest voltage guaranteed read as low |
| V_OH(min) | Lowest voltage a high output guarantees |
| V_OL(max) | Highest voltage a low output guarantees |

Between V_IL(max) and V_IH(min) is a forbidden zone where the input's behaviour isn't guaranteed.

An output can drive an input reliably only if:

```
V_OH(min) ≥ V_IH(min)   (high works)
V_OL(max) ≤ V_IL(max)   (low works)
```

The differences are the **noise margins**: how much noise the link can tolerate before a bit is misread.

### Real numbers from TI datasheets

From TI's SN74HC00 datasheet (Recommended Operating Conditions at V_CC = 4.5 V): V_IH(min) = 3.15 V, V_IL(max) = 1.35 V. HC inputs scale with supply voltage.

From TI's SN74HCT00 datasheet (V_CC = 4.5 V to 5.5 V): V_IH(min) = 2.0 V, V_IL(max) = 0.8 V. These are "TTL-compatible" thresholds, designed to accept lower-voltage highs.

Suppose a 3.3 V microcontroller output guarantees V_OH ≥ 2.4 V and V_OL ≤ 0.4 V. These are illustrative figures (they match the JEDEC LVTTL limits for 3.3 V logic at a 2 mA load, and many 3.3 V microcontrollers do better at light loads). Take the real ones from your chip's datasheet at your load current.

```python
def margins(voh, vol, vih, vil):
    hi = voh - vih   # high noise margin
    lo = vil - vol   # low noise margin
    return round(hi, 2), round(lo, 2)

# 3.3 V output into 74HC at 4.5 V
print(margins(2.4, 0.4, 3.15, 1.35))
# same output into 74HCT
print(margins(2.4, 0.4, 2.0, 0.8))
```

```
(-0.75, 0.95)
(0.4, 0.4)
```

The negative high margin means a 3.3 V output **isn't guaranteed** to be read as high by a 5 V HC input. It may work on your bench and fail on another day or another chip. The HCT part has positive margins in both states, which is why an HCT buffer powered from 5 V is a standard way to translate 3.3 V logic up to 5 V. TI's HCT application note (SCLA011) recommends HCT parts for the closely related problem of feeding TTL-level outputs into HC logic.

### The dangerous direction: 5 V into 3.3 V

Going down is the real hazard. A 5 V output driving a 3.3 V-only input exceeds that input's rating. Options, depending on speed and direction:

- A **level-shifter** chip designed for the job (the robust choice for fast or bidirectional signals).
- A **resistor divider** to scale 5 V down to about 3.3 V, for slow, one-way signals. Lesson 2's loading rules apply.
- An input the datasheet explicitly specifies as 5 V tolerant, under the stated conditions.

## Absolute maximum ratings versus recommended operating conditions

Every datasheet separates two very different tables.

**Absolute Maximum Ratings** are stress limits. The SN74HC00 datasheet's footnote is typical of TI's wording: "Stresses beyond those listed under Absolute Maximum Rating may cause permanent damage to the device. These are stress ratings only, which do not imply functional operation of the device at these or any other conditions beyond those indicated under Recommended Operating Condition. Exposure to absolute-maximum-rated conditions for extended periods may affect device reliability." For the SN74HC00 the table includes a supply maximum of 7 V and an input clamp current of ±20 mA.

**Recommended Operating Conditions** are where the part is guaranteed to work as specified: SN74HC00 V_CC from 2 V to 6 V, inputs between 0 and V_CC.

```diagram
 0V                                    7V
 |--- recommended: 2–6 V ---|          |
 |------- stress limit: 7 V -----------|
    not a guaranteed operating range
```

Design inside recommended conditions with margin. Never treat an absolute maximum as a target. Living near it can shorten the part's life even if it doesn't fail at once.

## Reading a datasheet

Datasheets follow a predictable layout. In order of usefulness to a beginner:

1. **Features and description:** what the part is, supply range, key specs.
2. **Pin configuration:** pin numbers and names. Note which **view** (top view is standard for ICs) and the pin 1 marking.
3. **Absolute maximum ratings:** what will damage it.
4. **Recommended operating conditions:** where to design.
5. **Electrical characteristics:** guaranteed min/max values under stated **test conditions**, such as V_OH at a given load current.
6. **Typical characteristics (graphs):** how the part usually behaves. Not guaranteed.
7. **Application and layout information:** example circuits, decoupling and layout advice. Often the most practical section.

Rules of thumb:

- **Design to min/max, not "typ".** Typical values describe an average part on a good day.
- **Read the test conditions.** A V_OH(min) at 20 µA isn't the same as at 4 mA. TI's SN74HC00 lists 4.4 V and 3.98 V respectively at V_CC = 4.5 V and 25 °C.
- **Read the footnotes.** They hold the exceptions.
- **Get the datasheet for the exact part number**, including suffixes, from the manufacturer.

## Protecting inputs

Inputs that connect to the outside world (jacks, long wires, other equipment) see accidents: wrong voltages, static discharge, hot-plugging.

Most CMOS chips have internal **clamp diodes** from each input to V_CC and to GND. When an input goes beyond a rail by a diode drop, the diode conducts and dumps the excess current into the rail.

```diagram
        VCC
         |
        ─┴─ clamp diode
  in ─[ R ]─┬──── chip input
        ─┬─ clamp diode
         |
        GND
```

A **series resistor** limits the current that flows into those clamps during a fault. TI's footnote reads: "The input and output voltage ratings may be exceeded if the input and output current ratings are observed." For example, a 10 kΩ series resistor with a 5 V fault on a 3.3 V input lets roughly (5 − 3.3 − ~0.5) / 10k ≈ 0.12 mA flow. The 0.5 V clamp drop is an assumption: the real drop depends on the chip and the current, and like any silicon junction it is usually somewhat higher at milliamp currents. Assuming a low drop is the cautious choice, because it overestimates the current.

Be conservative:

- **Clamps are fault protection, not a level shifter.** Some manufacturers, such as PJRC for Teensy 4.1, say plainly not to drive pins above 3.3 V. Use proper level conversion for normal operation.
- **Microcontrollers specify their own injected-current limits.** Check the chip's datasheet rather than borrowing a 74HC figure.
- **Back-powering:** a signal driven into an unpowered chip can power it partly through the clamp diodes, causing strange behaviour or damage. Power boards up together, or make sure signals can't arrive before the supply.
- **External Schottky clamps** (with a lower forward drop than the internal diodes) are often added on exposed inputs, so they conduct before the chip's internal diodes do.

## Decoupling capacitors

Digital chips draw current in very short pulses each time their transistors switch. The supply wiring has resistance and inductance, so it can't deliver those pulses instantly. The local supply voltage dips and rings, and that noise spreads to everything sharing the supply, including audio.

A **decoupling** (bypass) capacitor next to the chip's supply pin acts as a local reservoir, supplying the pulses so the long supply path doesn't have to. TI's SN74HC00 datasheet says: "Each VCC terminal should have a good bypass capacitor to prevent power disturbance. A 0.1-μF capacitor is recommended for this device." It also suggests 0.1 µF and 1 µF in parallel, placed "as close to the power terminal as possible".

Practical rules:

- **100 nF ceramic at every supply pin,** with short connections to the pin and to ground. Distance adds inductance and defeats the purpose.
- **Bulk capacitance** (an electrolytic, say 10–100 µF) where power enters a board, for slower load changes. Values are typical, not prescriptive; follow the datasheets.
- **Follow the datasheet** where it gives specific values. Audio codecs and regulators often do.

Lesson 7 explains why this matters even more for audio.

## Key takeaways

- Know each pin's voltage limits from the board and chip documentation. 5 V on a board doesn't mean 5 V-tolerant pins.
- An output drives an input reliably only if V_OH(min) ≥ V_IH(min) and V_OL(max) ≤ V_IL(max).
- 3.3 V into 5 V HC isn't guaranteed; an HCT buffer or level shifter fixes it. 5 V into 3.3 V-only pins can cause damage.
- Absolute maximums are damage limits. Design within recommended operating conditions.
- Design to guaranteed min/max under the stated test conditions, not to typical values.
- Series resistors and clamp diodes protect against faults. They aren't a substitute for proper level conversion.
- Put 100 nF of decoupling right at every chip's supply pin, plus bulk capacitance at the power entry.
